title: Agents vs. chatbots vs. workflows
notes: A chatbot replies, a workflow follows preset steps, and an agent chooses its steps.
If you can write the steps down, a workflow is usually cheaper and safer.
Use an agent when steps depend on the request. Many jobs don't need one.

slides.title: Agents vs. chatbots vs. workflows
slides.sub: Three ways to automate, one question to tell them apart
sentences: Agent is a popular word right now, and it gets stuck on almost everything.
In this lesson you will meet three different kinds of system: chatbots, workflows and agents.
By the end, you will know the one question that tells them apart, and when each one is the right choice.

slides.title: Who decides the steps?

cells: No steps: it replies, then waits
Yes, it picks tools as it goes

note.text: Who decides what happens next: a person in advance, or the model?

sentences: Here are the three, side by side.
A chatbot reads a message and writes a reply, and that's all: no lookups and no actions.
A workflow does take actions, but a person wrote every step in advance, and it follows them in order.
An agent takes actions too, but the model chooses which steps to take while it runs.
So the question that separates them is simple.
Who decides what happens next: a person who wrote it down in advance, or the model in the moment?

slides.title: A chatbot on its own

messages.label: Ana
messages.text: Hi, where is my order ORB-10482? It's been four days.

messages.label: FAQ chatbot
messages.text: I'm sorry, I can't access order information. Standard shipping takes 3 to 5 business days.

messages.label: Ana
messages.text: It's been FOUR days. Where is it?

messages.label: FAQ chatbot
messages.text: I'm sorry, I can't access order information.

aside.label: Good at
aside.text: Explaining what it already knows. Not facts it can't see.

sentences: First, the chatbot, which is what Orbit runs today.
Ana asks where her order is.
The bot answers politely, with the general shipping times from the FAQ page.
Ana asks again, more frustrated this time.
And she gets the same apology, because the bot has nothing new to look at.
Chatbots are good at explaining what they already know, like policies and product care, but they can't fetch facts they can't see.
Once you give a chatbot tools and let it choose when to use them, it is on its way to becoming an agent.

slides.title: A workflow: preset steps

note.text: Same three steps every time. Nothing to decide, so no model.

sentences: Next, a workflow, and Orbit could use one tomorrow.
When Sam's warehouse marks an order as shipped, the orders system announces it.
A template fills in the customer's name, the item and the tracking number.
And the email goes out to the customer.
Same three steps, every time, in the same order, with nothing to decide, so no language model is needed.
It runs in a second and costs almost nothing, and customers with a tracking number are less likely to ask where their order is.

slides.title: Workflow or agent?

right.label: Agent
points: Slower: each step is a model call
Can be wrong, needs limits and tests

sentences: So when should you use which?
If you can write the steps down ahead of time, use a fixed workflow.
It is fast and nearly free, it does the same thing every time, and it is easy to test.
Reach for an agent when the steps depend on the request.
Ana wants tracking, Grace wants a return, Owen wants a different size, and you can't predict the mix.
But agents are slower, every step is a paid model call, and they can make mistakes.
So they need limits and testing, and that is a big part of this course.

slides.title: Three Orbit jobs, three answers

cards.title: Owen's size swap
flow: Jacket too big, swap L for M?

sentences: Let's try the question on three real Orbit jobs.
An email every time an order ships: the steps never change, so it's a workflow.
A customer asks how to waterproof her boots: the answer is already written down, so a chatbot or a help page will do.
Owen wants to swap his jacket for a smaller size.
That needs his order, the stock level and the exchange policy.
What to check next depends on each answer, so it's a job for an agent.
One question sorted all three: who has to decide the steps?

slides.title: Honest advice: start simple
slides.lead: Use the simplest thing that works.

bullets.text: A clear FAQ page answers many questions for free
Use an agent only when steps depend on the request
Mix them: a workflow can call a model for one step

aside.label: Cost check
aside.text: Every agent step is a paid model call. It adds up fast.

sentences: Here is the honest advice experienced builders give.
Many repeat questions are answered perfectly well by a clear FAQ page, which costs nothing to run.
If the steps are known, build a workflow: it is cheaper, faster and more predictable.
Use an agent only when the steps really depend on the request.
And you can mix them: a workflow can call a model for a single step, like sorting an email into a category.
Keep cost in mind too, because every agent step is a paid model call, and Orbit gets hundreds of tickets a day.

slides.title: What to take away

points.text: Chatbot: replies with text, can't look anything up
Workflow: preset steps, the same every time
Agent: the model decides the steps and uses tools
Known steps? A workflow is usually cheaper and safer

sentences: Here is what to keep.
A chatbot replies with text, but it can't look anything up or act.
A workflow acts, following steps a person wrote in advance.
An agent acts too, but the model decides the steps as it goes.
If you can write the steps down, a workflow is usually the better and cheaper choice, and many jobs never need an agent.
Next, we look at where agents are earning their keep in real companies today.

midQuiz.q: What's the key difference between a workflow and an agent?
options: Only agents can send emails or update records
A person sets a workflow's steps, but an agent's model decides them
Workflows can never use a language model
midQuiz.explain: Both can act. The difference is who decides the steps: a person ahead of time, or the model.

midQuiz.q: Why does the FAQ chatbot keep apologising to Ana?
options: It has no way to look up her order
Its language model is too small
Ana didn't include her order number
midQuiz.explain: It understood her and had her order number. It has no connection to the orders system.
midQuiz.hint: Ana gave everything needed. What was the bot missing?

endQuiz.q: Leo wants a support channel alert for every one-star review. What fits best?
options: A workflow: new review, check stars, post the message
An agent that reads every review and decides what to do
A chatbot Leo can ask about reviews
endQuiz.explain: The trigger, check and action are known in advance. A workflow does it instantly and cheaply.
endQuiz.hint: Could you write every step down in advance?

endQuiz.q: Which is a good reason NOT to use an agent?
options: The answer depends on lookups that change per request
The steps are the same every time and can be written down
Customers phrase the same question in many ways
endQuiz.explain: Fixed steps suit a workflow. The other two are reasons an agent might help.
endQuiz.hint: Two make an agent useful. One makes it unnecessary.
